performers: Sviatoslav Richter; Warsaw National Philharmonic Orchestra; Stanisław Wisłocki
intro: The finale’s broad melody begins quietly with oboe and violas and ends blazing in C major across the orchestra. Sviatoslav Richter and Stanisław Wisłocki bring the concerto home through quick exchanges, a solo flourish and one last great song.

cues.title: The strings set off quietly
cues.text: The strings begin with little phrases that pass between violins and cellos. Clarinets, bassoons and a quiet tuba support them; the piano waits. The introduction moves from the Adagio’s E major back towards C minor.
cues.evidence: Gutheil full score, Boosey & Hawkes reprint, pp. 68–69: quiet strings, clarinets, bassoons and tuba. The E major to C minor route is described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Concerto_No._2_(Rachmaninoff).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Leaps, then short replies
cues.text: The piano bounds across the keyboard, then settles into short, accented figures. Flutes and clarinets answer, and the strings pluck their accompaniment. This first tune is quick on its feet.
cues.evidence: Full score, pp. 70–72: solo leaps, accented piano theme, flute and clarinet replies and pizzicato strings. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/7/72/IMSLP528309-PMLP01953-Rachmaninoff_-_Piano_Concerto_No._2_(orch._score).pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Oboe and violas, singing together
cues.text: Moderato: oboe and violas introduce the long B♭ major melody. The piano rests while horns hold the harmony and cellos and basses pluck underneath. After all the soloist’s quick work, the orchestra supplies the tune everyone remembers.
cues.evidence: Full score, p. 77: Moderato, B♭ major second theme for solo oboe and violas, horns and pizzicato lower strings.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Tolstoy withholds his blessing
cues.text: In early 1900 Rachmaninoff and the bass Feodor Chaliapin perform one of his songs for Leo Tolstoy, hoping for encouragement. Tolstoy asks: “Tell me, do you really think anybody needs music like that?”
cues.evidence: Marc Mandel’s BSO note recounts the early-1900 meeting and quotes Tolstoy’s response to Rachmaninoff and Chaliapin. https://www.bso.org/works/piano-concerto-no-2-6

cues.title: The short tune takes charge
cues.text: The first theme’s clipped figures return to the foreground. The piano strikes chords high on the keyboard while winds, brass and strings answer in sharp bursts. These little phrases will occupy most of the development.
cues.evidence: Full score, pp. 83–85: high piano chords and orchestral exchanges; the development’s reliance on the first theme is described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Concerto_No._2_(Rachmaninoff).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The song in D♭
cues.text: The long melody returns in D♭ major, carried by flute and first violins. The piano rests again before taking it up. The tune is a minor third higher than its first appearance, with brighter voices singing it.
cues.evidence: Full score, pp. 97–99: Moderato, D♭ major second theme for flute and first violins, then piano.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Full Moon and Empty Arms
cues.text: The finale’s long melody acquires another life as Full Moon and Empty Arms. Frank Sinatra records the song.
cues.evidence: Marc Mandel’s BSO note identifies the song’s source in the finale; Sinatra’s recording is documented in the concerto’s reception account. https://www.bso.org/works/piano-concerto-no-2-6 and https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Concerto_No._2_(Rachmaninoff)

cues.title: Quiet figures start the climb
cues.text: Short phrases pass through the woodwinds and strings. The piano joins softly, with poco a poco accelerando above its repeated figures. The bass begins to move, and the route to the final flourish gathers speed.
cues.evidence: Full score, p. 103 and following: orchestral fragments, piano entrance at p and poco a poco accelerando.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: C major, at last
cues.text: Maestoso: the long melody arrives in C major across winds and strings, above the piano’s full chords. Horns, trombones and tuba support it. The little oboe song now fills the orchestra.
cues.evidence: Full score, pp. 109–112: C major Maestoso, expanded wind and string melody, piano chords and lower-brass support.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: One last burst of speed
cues.text: Più vivo sets the piano moving again after the broad melody. Quick figures and repeated orchestral chords drive towards the final C major cadence. The concerto ends with four emphatic attacks.
cues.evidence: Full score, pp. 112–116: Più vivo, quick piano figures and final C major cadence with four-attack closing rhythm.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The piano bounds into C minor
transitions.to: A · Piano leaps and quick wind replies
transitions.how: The short string phrases grow into an orchestral crescendo. The piano sweeps in and then leaps between low bass notes and high figures in C minor. As its accented tune takes shape, flutes and clarinets answer over plucked strings.
transitions.evidence: Full score, pp. 68–72: introduction, solo flourish, first theme and pizzicato accompaniment.

transitions.title: Oboe and violas inherit the tune
transitions.from: A · Piano leaps and quick wind replies
transitions.to: B · Oboe and violas sing in B♭
transitions.how: A ritardando slows the piano’s broken chords. At Moderato, the soloist rests and oboe and violas begin the B♭ major melody. Horns hold quiet chords, while cellos and basses pluck the bass beneath the long phrase.
transitions.evidence: Full score, p. 77: ritardando, Moderato and the B♭ major oboe-and-viola theme.

transitions.title: The piano recovers its clipped figures
transitions.from: B · Oboe and violas sing in B♭
transitions.to: Dev · The short tune takes over
transitions.how: The lyrical group’s B♭ major close breaks into forceful exchanges. The piano climbs through a quick run and strikes high chords at ff; winds, brass and strings answer with short, accented phrases. The first theme’s small figures become the development’s main business.
transitions.evidence: Full score, pp. 83–85; the first-theme basis of the development is described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Concerto_No._2_(Rachmaninoff).

transitions.title: The returning song rises to D♭
transitions.from: Dev · The short tune takes over
transitions.to: B′ · Flute and violins sing in D♭
transitions.how: The piano slows through Meno mosso and a ritardando, then falls silent at Moderato. Flute and first violins bring back the long theme in D♭ major. Clarinets and bassoons hold the harmony while the lower strings pluck their bass notes.
transitions.evidence: Full score, p. 97: Meno mosso, ritardando and D♭ major Moderato with flute and violin melody.

transitions.title: Small phrases start to accelerate
transitions.from: B′ · Flute and violins sing in D♭
transitions.how: The long melody breaks into short wind and string phrases. The piano enters quietly over a held low C, with poco a poco accelerando above its repeated figures. Horns join the rhythm, the bass begins to move, and the passage gathers towards Presto.
transitions.evidence: Full score, pp. 103–108: orchestral fragments, quiet piano entrance over C, accelerando and Presto.

transitions.title: A solo flourish opens the final song
transitions.to: B″ · The long tune reaches C major
transitions.how: Presto brings a short orchestral blaze, then a long fermata over rests leaves the piano alone. Its flourish crosses the keyboard and slows into Maestoso. The second melody returns in C major, carried by winds and strings above full piano chords and a low C in the bass.
transitions.evidence: Full score, pp. 108–110: Presto, long orchestral rest, solo flourish and C major Maestoso.

source.title: Rachmaninoff, Piano Concerto No. 2, full score, Gutheil engraving in Boosey & Hawkes reprint, plate B. & H. 16674
source.locator: Printed pp. 68–116: orchestral introduction, quick piano theme, B♭ major oboe-and-viola melody, D♭ major return and C major Maestoso.

timeline.note: Quiet string phrases pass between violins and cellos, with clarinet, bassoon and tuba support (pp. 68–69).
The orchestra swells and the piano enters with a sweep across the keyboard (pp. 69–70).
The piano’s short, accented tune draws flute and clarinet replies over plucked strings (pp. 71–72).
The piano exchanges quick phrases with woodwinds, horns and strings (pp. 73–75).
Oboe and violas sing the B♭ major theme at Moderato; horns hold chords and lower strings pluck the bass (p. 77).
The piano takes the long melody above its own broken chords, with quiet woodwinds and strings (pp. 78–79).
The piano strikes high chords while winds, brass and strings answer in short bursts (pp. 83–85).
Wind and brass phrases gather around the piano’s running notes and chords (pp. 91–93).
Flute and first violins bring back the long tune in D♭ major; clarinets and bassoons hold the harmony (p. 97).
The piano takes up the D♭ major melody over sustained woodwind and string notes (pp. 98–99).
The full orchestra drives through Presto before a long pause leaves the piano alone (p. 108).
The piano’s solo flourish crosses the keyboard between Presto and Maestoso (pp. 108–109).
Winds and strings sing the C major Maestoso above piano chords, horns and lower brass; trumpets and cymbals rest (pp. 109–110).
At Più vivo, quick piano figures race towards full-orchestra chords with timpani, bass drum and cymbals (pp. 112–116).

quote.text: I feel like a ghost wandering in a world grown alien. I cannot cast out the old way of writing, and I cannot acquire the new.
quote.source: Rachmaninoff to Leonard Liebling, 1939; published in The Musical Courier, 5 April 1943

composer.background:
“My hearty thanks to the old man for not having forgotten about me!” Rachmaninoff wrote to the singer Mikhail Slonov on 26 December 1892. The old man was Tchaikovsky, who had praised his opera Aleko in a newspaper interview. Rachmaninoff was nineteen, newly graduated from the Moscow Conservatory with its Great Gold Medal. Tchaikovsky helped get the opera into the Bolshoi, and in May 1893 sat in the audience applauding. For a young composer, it was an excellent beginning.

His childhood had been less orderly. Born into a landowning family, he grew up at Oneg, near Novgorod, until his father’s financial failures forced a move to St Petersburg. He entered the Conservatory there in 1883. His parents separated; his sister Sofia died of diphtheria; schoolwork went badly. His grandmother took him to Orthodox services, where he heard the voices and bells that would stay with him. In 1885 his cousin Alexander Siloti recommended a move to Moscow, under the formidable care of the piano teacher Nikolai Zverev.
